title: Branding with Symbol and opaque types in JS
hook: Two strings both hold user IDs but must never be swapped. Branding adds a compile-time-only tag in TypeScript and a runtime Symbol marker in JavaScript so structurally identical values stay distinct in your API.

blocks.text: **Branding** (or **opaque types**) makes two values with the same runtime shape incompatible at the type level. TypeScript uses a phantom property like `readonly __brand: 'UserId'`. In plain JavaScript you can attach a **unique Symbol** property at creation time so only your factory produces valid values — a lightweight nominal tag. Symbols are **not enumerable**, so they do not leak into JSON.stringify unless you include them explicitly.

entries.plainDefinition: Phantom type tag preventing accidental mixing of primitives with the same underlying representation.
entries.example: type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: unique symbol };

entries.plainDefinition: ECMAScript primitive for unique property keys — each Symbol() is distinct.
Type whose construction is hidden — callers cannot forge the brand without your factory.
Global symbols like Symbol.iterator — protocol hooks, not branding secrets.

blocks.text: Payment systems confuse **accountId** and **transactionId**; auth code passes a raw JWT string where an opaque session token was required. Structural typing allows both strings everywhere. Branding catches swaps at compile time (TS) or makes forgery harder at runtime (Symbol-guarded factories). C# uses distinct **record** types or **strongly typed ids** wrappers — branding is the TS/JS idiom for the same intent without CLR nominal types.

blocks.title: Interview trap: brand at runtime?
blocks.body: TS brands erase — they do not exist in emitted JS. For runtime proof you need Symbol markers, class instances, or validation. Say both layers when asked.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Define secret Symbol
items.body: Module-scoped const VALID = Symbol('validated'); not exported.

items.title: Factory validates input
items.body: Parse email, UUID, etc. — throw if invalid.

items.title: Attach marker
items.body: Return Object.freeze({ value, [VALID]: true }) or wrap in closure.

items.title: Consumers check marker
items.body: Only trusted functions accept objects with VALID before use.

snippet.label: TypeScript branded primitive
snippet.explanation: Brand exists only for the compiler. Runtime value is still a string — pair with validation in UserId().

snippet.label: Runtime Symbol marker
snippet.explanation: Secret Symbol not exported — callers cannot forge validated wrapper without the factory.

snippet.label: C# strongly typed id
snippet.explanation: Nominal record wrapper — real runtime type distinct from string. TS brand is compile-only unless you add similar wrapper class.

snippet.label: Failure mode: JSON strips Symbol brands
snippet.explanation: Branding does not survive JSON. After network/storage, run schema validation again — senior gotcha.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming TS brands protect runtime security. Exporting the validation Symbol so anyone can forge markers. Using well-known Symbols for secrecy — they are global. Forgetting to re-brand after JSON.parse.

blocks.text: Use brands for **domain invariants** (UserId, Cents, ISO8601 string), not every string. In monorepos, export factory functions only — keep brand symbol private. For APIs crossing process boundaries, prefer server-issued opaque tokens (random bytes) over client-side Symbol branding. Combine zod.transform with branded types: parse then brand in one step.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming branded types exist at runtime in emitted JS. Not knowing JSON drops Symbol keys. Cannot map to C# strongly typed ids or explain when branding is overkill.

interviewTakeaways: TS brands are compile-time only — runtime still sees plain string unless you add wrappers.
Secret Symbol markers give lightweight runtime nominal tags in plain JS modules.
JSON.stringify removes Symbol keys — re-validate after wire transfer.
60s: Branding prevents swapping structurally identical values. TS phantom brand; JS Symbol factory; C# record wrapper. Brands do not survive JSON.
Follow-up: UserId vs OrderId both strings — how do you enforce at API and DB layers?
commonPitfalls: Treating TypeScript brands as runtime security without validation.
Exporting the Symbol used for validation so forgery is trivial.
Strong answer: compile brand + runtime factory, JSON re-parse, map to C# strongly typed id pattern.
